Gastrointestinal Disorders

Hepatic Disorders

Hepatic disease in the ED is less about naming every chronic diagnosis and more about finding synthetic failure, portal-hypertension complications, infection, toxin injury, encephalopathy, renal failure, and need for transplant-level care.

Board trap: Do not call altered mental status “just ammonia” until hypoglycemia, intracranial bleed, sepsis, renal failure, drugs, Wernicke, and electrolyte disorders are considered.

HEPATIC DISORDERS

INTRODUCTION AND EPIDEMIOLOGY

Tintinalli Ch80 covers acute hepatitis, chronic liver disease, fulminant liver failure, NAFLD, and cirrhosis complications including ascites, SBP, hepatorenal syndrome, coagulopathy, and hepatic encephalopathy. Biliary colic and variceal bleeding are handled elsewhere, but their complications still influence disposition.

PATHOPHYSIOLOGY

Acute hepatitis injures hepatocytes through infectious, toxic, or metabolic insults. Chronic disease replaces normal parenchyma with fibrosis and nodules, producing loss of metabolic/synthetic function, portal hypertension, ascites, and portosystemic shunting. Portal hypertension plus poor albumin/sodium handling creates ascites; bowel flora translocation then creates SBP risk. Encephalopathy reflects impaired nitrogen handling, shunting, inflammation, and sometimes cerebral edema in fulminant failure.

CLINICAL FEATURES

Key presentations include jaundice, nausea, vomiting, diarrhea, RUQ or epigastric pain, pruritus, bruising/bleeding, altered mental status, increased abdominal girth, edema, weakness, syncope, acholic stools, dark urine, melena, or hematemesis. Exam may show tender hepatomegaly, jaundice, sallow complexion, muscle wasting, Dupuytren contracture, palmar erythema, spider nevi, caput medusae, fluid wave, asterixis, or bleeding diathesis.

LABORATORY EVALUATION AND IMAGING

Tests separate hepatocyte injury, synthetic failure, catabolic dysfunction, and specific disease. AST/ALT reflect hepatocyte injury; bilirubin pattern helps classify prehepatic/hepatic/posthepatic jaundice; PT/INR and albumin reflect synthetic function; ammonia can support but not define encephalopathy; serologies and toxin levels clarify cause.

NONHEPATIC CAUSES OF ABNORMAL LIVER TESTS

Abnormal liver-associated tests are not always liver failure. Hypoalbuminemia occurs with malnutrition, nephrotic syndrome, and protein-wasting enteropathy. Alkaline phosphatase can derive from bone, placenta, intestine, kidney, and leukocytes. AST may rise with MI or rhabdomyolysis. Bilirubin rises in hemolysis and sepsis. PT prolongs with vitamin K deficiency, chronic antibiotics, and anticoagulants. Urine bilirubin/urobilinogen is too insensitive for ED liver screening.

IMAGING

US and CT evaluate hepatic lesions, obstruction, ascites, and alternative abdominal pathology. Bedside US identifies ascites and guides paracentesis; formal duplex Doppler is preferred for portal or hepatic vein thrombosis; head CT is used when coagulopathic liver patients have altered mental status or trauma concern.

ACUTE, CHRONIC, AND FULMINANT HEPATIC DISEASE

Acute hepatitis commonly causes nausea, vomiting, fever, jaundice, bilirubinuria, RUQ pain, and tender hepatomegaly. Chronic hepatitis/cirrhosis causes long-standing scarring with portal hypertension, edema, ascites, GI bleeding, encephalopathy, and synthetic failure. Fulminant hepatic failure is acute hepatic failure with encephalopathy and coagulopathy and can rapidly progress to cerebral edema, shock, hypoglycemia, renal failure, and death.

ACUTE HEPATITIS-VIRAL

Viral hepatitis is often self-limited but needs careful risk stratification, public health thinking, and follow-up. Rosen's serology table helps distinguish HAV, HBV, HCV, and HDV markers; HBV markers change over time, so isolated results must be interpreted in clinical context. HCV antibody does not distinguish acute from chronic infection and may lag early infection.

ACUTE HEPATITIS-TOXIC

Alcohol and acetaminophen are common toxic causes, but ED history must include medications, supplements, mushrooms, raw oysters, industrial toxins, and herbal products. Remove or treat the offending exposure, correct volume/electrolytes, check acetaminophen level when appropriate, and follow poisoning guidance for NAC or mushroom/toxin pathways.

CHRONIC HEPATITIS AND CIRRHOSIS

Chronic HBV/HCV, NAFLD, and alcohol-related disease may be silent for years. ED care treats complications: ascites, SBP, encephalopathy, coagulopathy, GI bleeding, renal failure, and electrolyte derangements; definitive antiviral or long-term cirrhosis care is usually outpatient or inpatient specialty-led.

ASCITES

Ascites causes abdominal distention and sometimes respiratory compromise. Large-volume ascites can be treated by paracentesis; anticoagulation status is considered, but cirrhosis-related INR alone does not automatically prohibit paracentesis. Albumin is recommended after large-volume removal in many protocols.

SPONTANEOUS BACTERIAL PERITONITIS

SBP is a life-threatening infection of ascitic fluid. Fever, abdominal pain, tenderness, vomiting, GI bleeding, encephalopathy, or first-diagnosed ascites should prompt paracentesis. Treat empirically while cultures are pending when criteria or high suspicion are present. Negative Gram stain does not exclude SBP.

HEPATIC ENCEPHALOPATHY

HE ranges from mild confusion to coma. Precipitants include GI bleeding, constipation, dehydration, hypovolemia, electrolyte disorders, infection, renal injury, sedatives, and medication changes. Treat airway risk, search for mimics, correct triggers, and reduce gut ammonia production with lactulose; rifaximin or other agents may be adjuncts.

HEPATORENAL SYNDROME

Hepatorenal syndrome is renal failure in cirrhosis or hepatic failure without intrinsic renal pathology, often after SBP. Type 1 progresses quickly with oliguria and creatinine doubling; type 2 is slower. It signals extreme morbidity and requires admission, volume assessment, infection treatment, and specialty care.

COAGULOPATHY

Coagulopathy from impaired synthetic function becomes dangerous with active bleeding or procedures. Vitamin K deficiency may respond to phytonadione; FFP and platelets are reserved for bleeding or procedural indications. Variceal hemorrhage belongs to the upper GI bleed pathway.

HEPATIC FAILURE

Acute liver failure commonly follows acetaminophen overdose, indeterminate injury, other drugs, hepatitis B, or autoimmune hepatitis. Hallmarks are encephalopathy, coagulopathy, renal failure, hypoglycemia, hypotension, immunodeficiency, and cerebral edema risk. Fulminant liver failure requires critical care and early consultation with a transplant center. Treat airway, shock, glucose/electrolytes, cerebral edema risk, bleeding, infection, and transfer needs.

NONALCOHOLIC FATTY LIVER DISEASE

NAFLD spans steatosis, steatohepatitis, cirrhosis, and liver failure. In the ED it is often incidental fatty liver or mild AST/ALT elevation in obesity/metabolic syndrome. Counsel alcohol avoidance, outpatient follow-up, weight loss, and exercise rather than starting unproven ED medications.

GENETIC AND AUTOIMMUNE LIVER DISORDERS

Gilbert syndrome causes intermittent bilirubin/liver test abnormalities without synthetic failure. Wilson disease, hemochromatosis, alpha-1 antitrypsin deficiency, autoimmune hepatitis, and primary biliary cirrhosis can cause chronic severe disease; ED care focuses on identifying decompensation and arranging specialty management.

PRE- AND POSTHEPATIC VENOUS THROMBOSIS

Portal vein thrombosis can produce colicky abdominal pain or be found incidentally; Budd-Chiari syndrome causes hepatic venous outflow obstruction with abdominal pain, hepatomegaly, ascites, and potential rapid fibrosis/liver failure. Doppler imaging and timely specialty consultation matter.

DISPOSITION AND FOLLOW-UP

Admit high-risk acute hepatitis: elderly or pregnant patients, inadequate response to supportive care, bilirubin >=20 mg/dL, PT 50% above normal, hypoglycemia, or GI bleeding. Admit chronic liver patients with respiratory compromise from ascites, abdominal pain, fever, acidosis, leukocytosis, SBP concern, new/worse encephalopathy, hepatorenal syndrome, coagulopathy with bleeding, or severe volume/sodium derangements. Decompensated cirrhosis is a safety problem as much as a lab problem. Discharge only if gait/safety, support, follow-up, and fall/bleeding risk are acceptable.

SPECIAL CONSIDERATIONS

PAIN CONTROL IN PATIENTS WITH HEPATIC DISEASE

Avoid NSAIDs in cirrhosis/chronic hepatitis because of GI and renal toxicity. Reduced-dose acetaminophen up to 2 g/day can be acceptable short term in selected patients. Gabapentin/pregabalin may help neuropathic pain. Avoid routine opioids; if unavoidable, use reduced dose/longer interval and avoid in encephalopathy or substance-use risk.

MEDICATION DOSE ADJUSTMENT

Cirrhosis changes bioavailability through shunting, low protein binding, high intestinal permeability, impaired motility, and reduced hepatic clearance. High extraction drugs need lower initial and maintenance dosing; intermediate extraction drugs start low-normal and reduce maintenance; low extraction drugs often keep initial dose but reduce maintenance.

PREGNANCY

Pregnant patients can have usual hepatic disease, but HELLP in late pregnancy or postpartum must be considered with RUQ/epigastric pain, elevated liver enzymes, hemolysis, or thrombocytopenia.

LIVER TRANSPLANT PATIENT

Liver transplant patients commonly present with metabolic or infectious problems; immunosuppression, graft issues, and atypical infection presentations require early specialty contact.

TRAVELERS AND GLOBAL CITIZENS

Travelers with abdominal pain, vomiting, diarrhea, fever, or jaundice may have parasitic or region-specific liver disease; travel and exposure history are mandatory.

PALLIATIVE CARE

End-stage liver disease can progress rapidly whether or not transplant is possible. Early goals-of-care discussions and palliative support are part of ED disposition planning.
